You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

You are analyzing one foundational paper in language model research for a research-group documentation task. The paper's arXiv ID is 2301.07041.

CONTEXT: Our group is building structured notes (to be posted to Notion) and a comparative Word report covering three papers: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv 2205.01068). Your job is to analyze ONLY the paper with arXiv ID 2301.07041.

HOW TO PROCEED:
1. Confirm the paper exists via mcp__arxiv_local__list_papers (it should be among the 3 stored papers). Read its full content with mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper (paper_id = 2301.07041). If that fails, try mcp__arxiv_local__download_paper first, or use the mcp__arxiv-latex__* tools (list_paper_sections, get_paper_section, get_paper_prompt, get_paper_abstract) to retrieve the text/sections.
2. Use mcp__arxiv-latex__list_paper_sections (arxiv_id = 2301.07041) to enumerate the paper's section structure.
3. Read the abstract, introduction, and all key sections (methodology, experiments, results, discussion, conclusion) thoroughly so your notes are grounded in the actual full text.

DELIVERABLE — return a structured report in EXACTLY this markdown format (do not add extra top-level sections):

## Paper: <exact paper title>
- arXiv ID: <id>
- Authors: <full author list as given>
- Abstract: <1-3 sentence summary in your own words>

### Section Structure
- <bulleted list of the paper's main sections/headings as found, e.g., 1. Introduction, 2. Background, ...>

### Main Contributions
- <3-6 bullets, each 1-2 sentences, describing the paper's primary contributions to LLM research>

### Methodology
- <a detailed paragraph or bullets (4-8 sentences total) describing how the work was done: models/datasets used, training setup, key techniques (e.g., power-law fits, RLHF pipeline, model suite sizes), evaluation approach>

### Key Findings
- <3-6 bullets, each 1-2 sentences, with concrete numbers/results where the paper provides them (e.g., loss scaling exponents, parameter counts, benchmark scores, human preference rates)>

### Relevance to LLM Research
- <1-2 sentences on why this paper matters / how it fits the broader LLM research narrative>

Be accurate and faithful to the paper text. Do NOT fabricate numbers or findings that are not in the paper. If a specific statistic cannot be found, say so explicitly. Return only the structured report above.

Create three structured Notion pages in the team's Notion workspace for a research-group documentation task. The workspace currently has NO existing pages or databases (search returns empty), so create the pages at the workspace root level using parent {"type": "workspace", "workspace": true} in mcp__notion__API-post-page. If the workspace-root parent is rejected, create a parent page titled "Paper Analysis" at workspace root first and then create the three paper pages as children of that parent page.

For each paper below, create a page whose TITLE is exactly "Paper: <paper title>" (note the "Paper: " prefix) and whose BODY contains structured notes with the specified content. Use headings (heading_2 or heading_3 blocks) for each subsection and bulleted_list_item blocks for bullet lists, mirroring the structure shown. Content must be accurate to the paper analysis provided — do not add or invent facts.

=====================
PAGE 1
Title: Paper: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
Body:
- Paragraph: "arXiv ID: 2301.07041 | Authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan"
- Heading: "Abstract" — paragraph: "This paper studies empirical scaling laws for language model performance, measured by cross-entropy loss, showing that loss scales as a power-law in model size, dataset size, and training compute, with trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Architectural details such as width/depth have minimal effect within a wide range, and simple equations govern overfitting and training-speed dependence, enabling optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget."
- Heading: "Main Contributions" with bullets:
  * "Establishes empirical power-law scaling laws for language model cross-entropy loss as a function of model size, dataset size, and compute budget."
  * "Derives simple closed-form equations (e.g., L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N) governing overfitting versus model/dataset size and training speed versus model size."
  * "Shows architectural choices (network width, depth) have minimal effects on loss within a wide range, making scale the dominant factor."
  * "Provides a principled framework for predicting model performance and optimally allocating a fixed compute budget across model size and data."
  * "Demonstrates that larger models are more sample-efficient than smaller ones."
- Heading: "Methodology" — paragraph: "The study is purely empirical: the authors trained a large suite of models (over 1000 models spanning roughly three orders of magnitude in scale) and fit power-law relationships to the resulting cross-entropy loss. Performance is characterized by the cross-entropy loss L, modeled as a power law in the number of parameters N (constant N_c and exponent alpha_N), with analogous power-law forms for dataset size D and compute C. The fitted exponents are approximately alpha_N = 0.076, alpha_D = 0.095, and alpha_C = 0.050. Evaluation is based on loss as a function of scale; the derived relationships are then used to reason about optimal compute-budget allocation and sample efficiency."
- Heading: "Key Findings" with bullets:
  * "Loss follows a power law in model parameters, L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N, with exponent alpha_N ≈ 0.076; analogous power laws hold for dataset size (alpha_D ≈ 0.095) and compute (alpha_C ≈ 0.050)."
  * "Scaling trends span more than seven orders of magnitude, indicating the power-law behavior is extremely robust across scales."
  * "Within a wide range, architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects on scaling behavior."
  * "Larger models are more sample-efficient: given fixed data, larger models achieve lower loss."
  * "The scaling relationships permit determination of the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget."
- Heading: "Section Structure" — paragraph: "Introduction; Scaling Laws; Experiments; Conclusion."
- Heading: "Relevance to LLM Research" — paragraph: "This paper is foundational: it established that model performance is predictable from scale alone, giving the field quantitative rules for choosing model size, dataset size, and compute. It directly underlies subsequent compute-optimal training analyses and the practice of planning model training budgets before training begins, shaping how modern LLMs are sized and trained."

=====================
PAGE 2
Title: Paper: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
Body:
- Paragraph: "arXiv ID: 2203.11171 | Authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang (canonical listing includes additional co-authors)"
- Heading: "Abstract" — paragraph: "Starting from GPT-3, the authors train language models that are much better at following user instructions by fine-tuning with supervised learning on demonstration data and then with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The resulting InstructGPT models are preferred by human labelers to GPT-3 outputs, are more truthful, and are less toxic, despite having only 1.3B parameters compared to the 175B GPT-3."
- Heading: "Main Contributions" with bullets:
  * "Introduces the three-step RLHF alignment pipeline — supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstrations, reward model training from human preference comparisons, and PPO fine-tuning against the reward model — as a practical method for aligning LLM behavior with human intent."
  * "Demonstrates that alignment can come from a much smaller model: InstructGPT 1.3B outputs are preferred over GPT-3 175B outputs by human evaluators on 85% of prompts, showing instruction-following quality does not require the largest model."
  * "Shows RLHF improves truthfulness (better performance on TruthfulQA) and reduces toxicity relative to the base GPT-3 models."
  * "Establishes that RLHF yields substantial alignment improvement with minimal trade-off in general capabilities."
- Heading: "Methodology" — paragraph: "The work starts from GPT-3 and applies a three-step RLHF procedure. Step 1 is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstration data to teach the model to follow instructions. Step 2 trains a reward model from human preference comparisons over model outputs. Step 3 fine-tunes the model with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) using the learned reward model as the training signal. The resulting InstructGPT models (highlighted at 1.3B parameters) are evaluated through human preference evaluations on user prompts, plus truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and toxicity benchmarks, with comparisons against the 175B GPT-3."
- Heading: "Key Findings" with bullets:
  * "Human evaluators prefer InstructGPT 1.3B outputs to GPT-3 175B outputs on 85% of prompts."
  * "InstructGPT models are more truthful (better on TruthfulQA) than GPT-3 and produce less toxic outputs."
  * "RLHF provides a substantial improvement in alignment with minimal trade-off in general capabilities."
  * "Model size is not the primary driver of perceived output quality: a 1.3B-parameter aligned model beats a 175B-parameter unaligned model in human preference."
- Heading: "Section Structure" — paragraph: "Introduction; Method; Experiments; Results."
- Heading: "Relevance to LLM Research" — paragraph: "This paper is the canonical RLHF/instruction-tuning reference that established the alignment paradigm underlying modern assistant models, showing how human feedback can make smaller models more helpful, truthful, and safe than far larger unaligned models. It bridges the scaling-laws era (optimal capabilities from scale) and the instruction-following era (behavioral control through human feedback)."

=====================
PAGE 3
Title: Paper: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models
Body:
- Paragraph: "arXiv ID: 2205.01068 | Authors: Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal (paper's full author list is longer)"
- Heading: "Abstract" — paragraph: "OPT is a suite of fully open-source large language models spanning 125M to 175B parameters. The models match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks while being publicly released, and the paper documents the training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale, along with release of model weights and training code."
- Heading: "Main Contributions" with bullets:
  * "Introduces OPT, an open-source suite of transformer language models spanning 125M to 175B parameters, making large-scale LLMs accessible to the research community."
  * "Demonstrates that open-source models at this scale can match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks (OPT-175B matches GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot benchmarks)."
  * "Releases full model weights and training code publicly, enabling the community to study large language models."
  * "Documents practical training methodology and hardware infrastructure (tensor and pipeline parallelism on large GPU clusters), including lessons learned from training at scale."
- Heading: "Methodology" — paragraph: "OPT uses a standard transformer architecture with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, trained with the AdamW optimizer. The models were trained on a combination of Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets totaling 800GB of text. Training used tensor and pipeline parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs. Evaluation compared OPT-175B against GPT-3 on zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks."
- Heading: "Key Findings" with bullets:
  * "OPT models range from 125M to 175B parameters, matching GPT-3's largest scale (175B)."
  * "OPT-175B matches GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks."
  * "The training corpus totaled 800GB of text drawn from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other sources."
  * "Training was scaled to up to 992 A100 GPUs using tensor and pipeline parallelism."
  * "The models achieve GPT-3-comparable performance while being fully open-source, with weights and code released."
- Heading: "Section Structure" — paragraph: "Introduction; Architecture; Training; Results."
- Heading: "Relevance to LLM Research" — paragraph: "This paper is a landmark open-source contribution: it demonstrated that GPT-3-scale performance (175B parameters) could be achieved and publicly released, breaking the closed-model paradigm of earlier frontier LLMs. It democratizes large language model research by providing weights, code, and engineering lessons (e.g., parallelism on 992 A100 GPUs, 800GB corpora)."

DELIVERABLE: Create all three pages. Then verify by calling mcp__notion__API-post-search with query "Paper:" and report back: (1) the page IDs and URLs of the three created pages, (2) confirmation that each page title is exactly "Paper: <title>", (3) how many pages were successfully created. If any page fails, retry once, then report the error precisely.
